common_name: Roman Candle Podocarpus (Variegated Columnar Yew Pine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this narrow, columnar selection holds its variegated new growth best with consistent moisture during its first two seasons.

directions: This patented Southern Living Plant Collection selection sends up narrow, upright stems tipped with creamy white new growth that matures to deep green, giving the plant a two-toned, candle-like appearance with each flush. Its tight, columnar habit needs little pruning to hold a formal vertical line, making it a useful living accent flanking an entry or filling a narrow side-yard bed where a wide shrub would crowd the space. Like other yew podocarpus selections it shrugs off heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, and deer generally leave it alone. Grow it in full sun for the brightest variegation, though it also holds reasonable color in light afternoon shade.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Mood Ring Podocarpus (Bronze-Red New Growth Yew Pine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; expect the most vivid bronze-pink flush on plants grown in full sun.

directions: Mood Ring is a patented Southern Living Plant Collection introduction selected for the bronze-pink flush its new needles take on in spring and again in cooler fall weather, settling to glossy dark green as they mature. Its dense, upright, slightly conical habit fills in fast enough for a hedge or privacy screen yet stays narrow enough for foundation beds and large containers. It shares the drought and heat tolerance of the species once its roots are established and needs only light shearing to keep a tidy outline. Full sun brings out the strongest seasonal color, though the plant also performs well in partial shade during the hottest Gulf Coast summers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the brightest gold flush develops on new growth in sunnier spots and mellows to green as needles age.

directions: Aurea is an older, narrowly upright selection of yew podocarpus grown for the bright yellow flush of its emerging needles, which age to green over the course of a season and create a two-tone effect on actively growing plants. Its slow, columnar growth habit makes it useful as a specimen or narrow screen where the seasonal gold color can be appreciated up close rather than lost in a mass planting. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and the sandy or clay soils common across the Gulf Coast about as well as the plain green species. Light shaping in late winter, before the spring flush, keeps the plant dense without sacrificing the fresh color show that follows.

common_name: Dwarf Japanese Plum Yew (Compact Mounding Cephalotaxus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is quite slow, so allow ample room for the eventual wide mound rather than crowding new plantings.

directions: This slow-growing dwarf form of Japanese plum yew builds a dense, rounded mound of soft, dark green, needle-like foliage that spreads wider than it grows tall, often taking a decade or more to reach four feet. It excels in deep shade beneath established trees where turf and most flowering shrubs struggle, tolerating root competition and low light far better than true yews or most needled evergreens. In regions with hot summers it prefers consistent shade, while in cooler climates it tolerates considerably more sun without scorching. Once established it needs little more than occasional watering during drought and is rarely bothered by deer, insects, or disease.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, average garden soil in partial shade; branches sprawl and semi-weep as the plant ages, so give it generous lateral room or let it drape over a low wall.

directions: Drupacea is a low, wide-spreading form of Japanese plum yew whose branches take on a soft, semi-weeping posture as the plant matures, sprawling outward far more than it rises. Its low profile and generous spread suit it to draping over retaining walls, softening the base of foundation plantings, or filling a broad shaded bank where an upright conifer would look out of place. Like other plum yew selections it tolerates deep shade, root competition from mature trees, and the heat and humidity of Southern summers far better than boxwood or true yew. It requires little pruning to keep its naturally loose, informal form and is essentially untroubled by deer, pests, or disease.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
